1149.title: the Rudram
1149.hook: the Rudram bows to the short and the tall, the eldest and the youngest, and even the middle child
1149.howItsDone: Chanters learn the Namakam's paired lines (namo jyeshthaya cha kanishthaya cha and others) by heart, usually from a teacher, and recite them in Vedic Sanskrit at home, in temples and in group chanting.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rudram gave us its heartbeat: namah, a bow, said again and again.
screen: `NAMAH — A BOW.` · `TODAY: WHO GETS THE BOW.`

segments.voice: Some family photos have a pecking order. The eldest stands in the middle, the youngest gets pulled onto someone's lap, and the middle one is near the edge, half out of frame. Partway through the Rudram, the hymn walks right into that photo. It bows to the eldest. It bows to the youngest. Then it does something families don't always do. It bows to the middle one too.
screen: `A FAMILY PHOTO.` → `THE MIDDLE ONE, HALF OUT OF FRAME.` → `THE HYMN BOWS TO ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: In one stretch of the Namakam, the bows come in pairs. A bow to the short one, and to the dwarf. To the large one, and to the one grown old. To the eldest, and to the youngest. To the firstborn, and to the one born after. To the middle one, and to the one not yet grown, still young and unsure. Rudra is all of them. Short and tall, old and young, first and last: these are the measures people use to rank each other. The hymn doesn't erase the differences. It names every one. But it bows to every one with the same small word, the same weight. Nobody's namah is louder. The eldest doesn't get a longer line. That fits what the Rudram has been doing all along. It found Rudra in the sun the cowherds see. Here it finds him in the whole family. There's a gentleness in that last pair. The Sanskrit word there points to someone not yet bold, not yet sure of themselves. A hymn to a fierce god stops to bow to the shy one. On the hymn's terms, the kid at the end of the table is no less holy than the grandparent at the head. The bow doesn't go up the ladder. It goes to every rung.
screen: `THE SHORT AND THE TALL.` · `THE ELDEST AND THE YOUNGEST.` · `THE MIDDLE ONE, AND THE SHY ONE.` · `THE SAME BOW FOR EVERY RUNG.` · then, large: `NOBODY'S NAMAH IS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people in your family, or the family you've made, from the eldest you can think of down to the youngest, and give each one a breath and the same inward bow. If one is harder to bow to, stay a little longer with that one. If you pray, you can say namah for each of them.
The Rudram. Today's lines: a bow to the eldest and the youngest, the firstborn and the later-born, the middle one and the shy one.

segments.voice: Your line: the Rudram. The shy one gets the same bow as the eldest. Go gently.

1150.title: the Rudram
1150.hook: the Rudram bows to the trees with green hair, to rain and to drought, to the well and to the foam
1150.howItsDone: The Rudram's lines about trees, rain and water are chanted in Vedic Sanskrit as part of the whole Namakam; it is recited during abhishekam in Shiva temples.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rudram bowed down a whole family: the eldest, the youngest, the middle one and the shy one.
screen: `THE ELDEST AND THE YOUNGEST.` · `TODAY: THE LAND AND THE SKY.`

segments.voice: A puddle on the sidewalk after a storm. A skin of foam where it meets the curb. New grass pushing through a crack. Nobody stops for any of it; it's the leftover stuff of weather. The Rudram stops for all of it. It bows to the foam, to the young grass, to the rain, and then, just as carefully, to the drought. Today the hymn goes outside.
screen: `A PUDDLE, A SKIN OF FOAM.` → `NEW GRASS IN A CRACK.` → `THE HYMN GOES OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Early in the Namakam there's a line that sounds almost like a fairy tale. A bow to the trees, the green-haired ones. The leaves are Rudra's hair. Then the bows spread across the whole land and sky. A bow to the one in the clouds, and to the one in the lightning. To the one in the rain, and to the one where no rain falls. To the one in wells, and to the one in pits in the ground. To the one in the young grass, and to the one in the foam. Notice the pairs again. Rain and no rain: the second half is the surprise. It's easy to find a god in the rain that feeds the crops. It's harder to bow to drought. The Rudram does both, with the same word. This is the fierce archer from the opening. The hymn doesn't pretend the land is only gentle: storms are his, lightning is his, the dry season is his. But it doesn't treat the wild places as godless either. Some readers hear this stretch as a long line of places to greet. Not because everything is pleasant. Because nothing is outside Rudra. The trees have green hair. The foam is holy. And dry ground that hasn't seen rain in a long time still gets its namah.
screen: `THE TREES, THE GREEN-HAIRED ONES.` · `CLOUD AND LIGHTNING, WELL AND PIT.` · `RAIN, AND NO RAIN.` · `NOTHING OUTSIDE RUDRA.` · then, large: `THE FOAM IS HOLY.`

segments.voice: Notice what the weather is doing right now, sun, cloud, rain, wind or still air, by looking out, listening, or feeling the temperature on your skin, and pleasant or not, offer it a small inward bow. Then think of one place outdoors you'd never look at twice, a ditch, a gutter, a patch of weeds, and bow to that too. If you pray, you can say namah for each.
The Rudram. Today's lines: a bow to the green-haired trees, to cloud and lightning, to rain and to drought, to the well, the grass and the foam.

segments.voice: Your line: the Rudram. Rain and no rain are both his. Rest well.

1151.title: the Rudram
1151.hook: after all the bowing, the Rudram's companion turns around and asks, line after line, and to me
1151.howItsDone: When the Shri Rudram is chanted in full, tradition pairs the Namakam with the Chamakam, and both are recited in Vedic Sanskrit, at home, in temples and during abhishekam.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rudram went outdoors: green-haired trees, rain and drought, foam at the edge of the water.
screen: `THE FOAM IS HOLY.` · `TODAY: THE OTHER HALF.`

segments.voice: Rice. Barley. Beans. Sesame. Wheat. Lentils. It sounds like a grocery list taped to a fridge. It's a Vedic hymn. When the Rudram is chanted in full, tradition pairs the bowing half, the Namakam, with a companion, the Chamakam. And the Chamakam does something the Namakam never did. It asks, line after line, ending again and again with two small words: cha me. And to me.
screen: `RICE, BARLEY, BEANS, SESAME.` → `A GROCERY LIST?` → `CHA ME — AND TO ME.`

segments.voice: The Namakam is built on namah, a bow. The Chamakam is built on cha me, and to me: a long list of requests, each tagged with those two words. What it asks for is startling in how ordinary it is. Strength, and to me. Ease and comfort. What is dear. Then food: milk and the sap of plants, ghee and honey, rice and barley, beans and sesame, wheat and lentils. Plowing, and rain. And two worth stopping on: eating together, and drinking together. The hymn asks for company at the table. There's something honest in that. After bowing to Rudra in every corner of the world, the chanter doesn't pretend to need nothing. Grain in the pot. Rain on the field. People to share it with. One way to hear the two halves is as breathing. The Namakam breathes out: everything belongs to Rudra, and I bow. The Chamakam breathes in: from all that, may this come to me. A life of only bowing could float away from the kitchen. A life of only asking would forget whom it's asking. There's no shame in it: the chanter who bowed to Rudra in the drought and the lightning now asks plainly for lentils. The hymn that bows to the storm sits right beside the one that asks for dinner, and for someone to eat it with.
screen: `CHA ME — AND TO ME.` · `GRAIN, RAIN, GHEE AND HONEY.` · `EATING TOGETHER, DRINKING TOGETHER.` · `BOWING OUT, ASKING IN.` · then, large: `ASKING FOR LENTILS.`

segments.voice: Without judging the list, let a few plain needs come up, not big wishes but ordinary things: sleep, a good meal, someone to eat it with, rain if your garden is dry. Name each one quietly and hold it out, the way the Chamakam does, then let the list go on the out-breath. If you pray, you can offer these needs to Shiva, in your own words.
The Rudram. Today, its companion, the Chamakam: cha me, and to me, asking plainly for grain, rain, and company at the table.

segments.voice: Your line: the Rudram. Bowing out, asking in. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1152.title: the Rudram
1152.hook: the hymn leaves the page and goes into the temple, where it is chanted while water pours over the stone
1152.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1152.howItsDone: In Shiva temples and in homes, Hindus may chant the Rudram during abhisheka, pouring water, milk and other offerings over the linga; some families arrange a Rudrabhisheka for a festival, a new home, or a hard time.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rudram's companion asked: cha me, and to me, right down to grain and a shared meal. Today is our last day inside the hymn.
screen: `THE RUDRAM, ONE LAST TIME.`

segments.voice: A small brass pot hangs on a chain above a stone linga. There's a pinhole in its base, and water drips, one drop and then the next, onto the stone. In some Shiva temples that drip is kept going through the day. On festival days it grows louder: priests sit close around the linga, and while water and milk are poured over it, they chant. One of the hymns they may chant is the Rudram. It was never only something to read. It's something to pour to. Today we follow it out of the book and into the bath.
screen: `A POT, A PINHOLE, A STONE.` → `PRIESTS CHANT AS THE WATER POURS.` → `OUT OF THE BOOK, INTO THE BATH.`

segments.voice: The bath is called abhisheka, and when the Rudram is chanted with it, people call the rite Rudrabhisheka. Hold the hymn next to the water and its shape shows. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, his arrow, his bow and his arms, and asks that the arrow be turned away and the bow unstrung. Then it keeps bowing, and finds Rudra everywhere: in forest and field, among carpenters and chariot-makers, even, startlingly, as the lord of thieves. Nothing is left outside the bow. Deep inside comes the line namah shivaya cha shivataraya cha: salutation to the kind one, and to the one kinder still. A traditional saying goes: the Rudram sits at the heart of the Vedas, the five syllables namah shivaya at the heart of the Rudram, and the two syllables shi-va at the heart of those five. Take it as a picture, not a measurement. The movement is real either way: from a god with a drawn bow, inward, toward a name that means auspicious, gentle, kind. The water makes the same movement. Another old saying: Vishnu loves to be adorned, Shiva loves to be bathed. The one with fire in his third eye and poison held in his throat is offered coolness, again and again. Hymn and pouring do one job: they meet the frightening edge of things with a bow, one drop at a time, until it shows a kind face.
screen: `ABHISHEKA: THE SACRED BATH.` · `IT OPENS WITH RUDRA'S ANGER.` · `SHIVA SITS AT ITS HEART.` · `SHIVA LOVES TO BE BATHED.` · then, large: `TO THE KIND ONE, AND KINDER STILL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels fierce right now, a worry, a person, a deadline with its bow drawn, and without fighting or fixing it, picture cool water poured slowly over it on each out-breath. Let the thing stay what it is, and just keep pouring. If you pray, you can say namah shivaya softly with each pour, or the name of God you use.
The Rudram. A Vedic hymn that bows to the fierce Rudra again and again, until Shiva, the kind one, appears at its heart. Today, chanted while the water pours.

segments.voice: Your line: the Rudram. Tomorrow, a great night of Shiva. See you then.

1153.title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1153.word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1153.hook: a festival kept in the dark, without food, awake until morning: a night with a syllabus
1153.carry: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1153.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
1153.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep it may fast, visit Shiva temples or worship at home, offer water, milk and bilva leaves to the linga, and stay awake through the night with chanting and singing.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, we left the Rudram where it lives: chanted while water pours over the stone. Now the night.
screen: `THE RUDRAM, POURED OVER STONE.` · `NOW THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Diwali fills a night with lamps. Holi fills a morning with color. Maha Shivaratri asks for something stranger. Don't eat. Don't sleep. Stay up in the dark, through the hours when the house goes quiet, and keep your attention on one thing until the sky starts to gray. No fireworks. The reward, if there is one, comes at dawn, to someone tired and hungry and still there. You've met this night through its stories: the hunter in the tree, the pillar of fire. This week we take the night itself as a course of study.
screen: `DON'T EAT. DON'T SLEEP.` → `ATTENTION ON ONE THING TILL DAWN.` → `THE NIGHT ITSELF, AS A COURSE.`

segments.voice: The name says it plainly. Maha, great. Shiva. Ratri, night. Tradition places it in the dark half of the lunar month, on the night just before the new moon, when there's almost no moon to see by. The Shiva Purana describes a vow for this night. Fast through the day. Worship Shiva in the linga, with water and bilva leaves. Stay awake until morning. That's the whole syllabus, short enough to fit on a card. But notice what kind of teaching it is. Nobody hands you a book or gives a lecture. The night teaches through the body. Hunger is one lesson, sleepiness another, the dark a third. Each takes away something you usually lean on, food, rest, light, and asks what's left to lean on instead. Some readers hear the near-moonless sky that way too: the mind's usual light gone, and only one thing worth turning toward. So we'll go through the night in order: the morning vow, the fast, keeping awake, the name repeated in the dark, the offerings, and dawn. One piece a day. Some people keep every hour in a temple crowded until sunrise. Some keep part of it at home. Some only learn about it. The course is the same either way. Its first lesson: the night isn't an empty space between two days. On this night, the night is the point.
screen: `MAHA, SHIVA, RATRI.` · `FAST, WORSHIP, STAY AWAKE.` · `THE NIGHT TEACHES THROUGH THE BODY.` · `ONE PIECE OF THE NIGHT A DAY.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Dim the light around you if you can, or simply close your eyes, and notice what the dark takes away, the screen, the faces, and what it gives back: sounds you hadn't heard, the weight of your body, the breath. Keep your attention on one thing, the breath is enough, and come back to it whenever you drift. If you pray, you can hold Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as that one thing.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, taken this week as a night curriculum. Today, its shape: a fast, worship, and staying awake until dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday began Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum: a fast, worship, and staying awake until dawn. Today, lesson one.
screen: `THE SHAPE OF THE NIGHT.` · `LESSON ONE.`

segments.voice: The great night of Shiva starts in daylight. On the morning of Shivaratri, after a bath, someone who means to keep the night takes a little water into the cupped right palm. They say, aloud or under the breath, where they are, what day it is, who they are, and what they're about to do: I will keep this fast, I will keep this night. Then they let the water go. Everything later, at three in the morning, when the body begs for food and sleep, leans on those words said in the light. The course begins with signing up.
screen: `WATER IN THE CUPPED PALM.` → `I WILL KEEP THIS NIGHT.` → `THE COURSE BEGINS BY SIGNING UP.`

segments.voice: That moment has a name: sankalpa, a resolve, an intention made on purpose. What it begins is a vrata, a vow kept for a set time. In the Shiva Purana's telling, the devotee rises early, bathes, and takes the vow before the fast and the vigil begin. Why decide so early? Because the hours you'll need it are the hours you can't decide well. At two in the morning almost any reason to quit sounds wise. So the tradition puts the deciding in daylight, when the mind is clear, and lets the night carry it out. The water helps too. Words can float away. Water poured from your hand can't be poured back, so the resolve becomes something the body did. Behind it sits an old idea. The Chandogya Upanishad says a person is made of resolve: as you resolve in this world, so you become. A sankalpa is that idea, shrunk to one day. And a vow is personal. Some fast completely. Some take only fruit and milk. Some keep the whole night in a temple, some part of it at home. The vow that counts is the one you actually said. So the first lesson is honesty about what you'll do, said clearly enough to hold yourself to later. A night with no resolve is just a late night. A night promised in the morning becomes a practice.
screen: `SANKALPA: A RESOLVE.` · `DECIDE IN DAYLIGHT.` · `WATER CAN'T BE POURED BACK.` · `THE VOW YOU ACTUALLY SAID.` · then, large: `AS YOU RESOLVE, SO YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Choose one small, honest thing you'll do before tomorrow, a meal eaten slowly or ten minutes without the phone, and say it quietly to yourself with where you are and what day it is, with a little water in your palm if there's a glass nearby. Then let the water go, into a plant or a sink, and sit with what you've promised. If you pray, you can offer the resolve to Shiva, or to the God you know.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum, lesson one: the sankalpa, a resolve made in daylight with water in the palm. Today closes the week.
screen: `THE SANKALPA, MADE IN DAYLIGHT.` · `THE WEEK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: On the day of Shivaratri, in some kitchens, the stove is still on. The food has just changed. No rice, no wheat, no lentils. Instead, sago pearls softening with potato and crushed peanuts, a bowl of fruit, a glass of milk. In other homes nothing goes on the stove, and people take only water until the next morning. Different vows, different tables. But in each, the stomach speaks up, in the afternoon, the evening, around midnight. Today's lesson is what to do when it rings.
screen: `THE KITCHEN CHANGES.` → `DIFFERENT VOWS, DIFFERENT TABLES.` → `THE STOMACH SPEAKS UP.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word for a fast is upavasa. Some teachers hear in it the sense of staying near, and read the fast that way: not going without, but keeping close to the one the night is for. Look at what a fast does on this night. First, it clears space. No meals to cook, serve and clean up means hours handed back, and the vow spends them on worship. Second, it turns hunger into a bell. Each pang can be met with one question: why am I awake? The ringing keeps calling the mind home. Third, a fast is held inside a vow, not a punishment. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all. So a household keeping Shivaratri can make room for children, for the sick, and for anyone a fast would hurt. A glass of milk taken honestly under the vow is still the vow. Now look back at the week. The Rudram bowed to the short and the tall, to trees and foam, then asked, and to me, and we left it chanted as water poured over the stone. Then the night opened: its shape, the morning resolve, and now the fast. A fierce thing, met with a bow. A long night, met with a promise. Hunger, met with a question. Each time, something hard is turned into attention.
screen: `UPAVASA: STAYING NEAR.` · `A FAST CLEARS SPACE.` · `HUNGER BECOMES A BELL.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT NONE AT ALL.` · then, large: `THE HARD THING BECOMES ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later something will tug at you, an itch, a thought of food, the urge to check a message; don't act on it or fight it, just ask quietly, why am I sitting here, and come back to the breath. Each tug is one more ring of the bell, and one more return. If you pray, you can let each return carry Shiva's name, or the name of God you use.
